title: Recursive CTEs
subtopics: Working with trees and graph-like relationships
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Recursive CTEs.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to anchor queries and recursive terms.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Recursive CTEs. Its primary job is to help you organize multi-stage SQL into views, CTEs and reusable reporting patterns that remain understandable. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing recursive ctes teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: organize multi-stage SQL into views, CTEs and reusable reporting patterns that remain understandable. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Recursive CTEs”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Anchor queries and recursive terms”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Anchor queries and recursive terms”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Recursive CTEs, with an explanation of “Anchor queries and recursive terms”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Recursive CTEs fits into the broader goal to organize multi-stage SQL into views, CTEs and reusable reporting patterns that remain understandable.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Anchor queries and recursive terms, Traversing hierarchical data, Recursive termination.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
